non_verbatim_nodes.text: On-call's first signal was a wave of database connection errors from the payments service.
Connection errors were the first visible signal, so on-call assumed pool exhaustion from traffic and spent the first twenty minutes on that assumption.
At 14:24 the pool size was raised from 50 to 150.
Error rates dropped noticeably afterward, which felt like confirmation that pool exhaustion was the root cause.
Error rates had not fully returned to normal, so a slower secondary investigation kept going in parallel.
Query-level tracing showed the payments service's customer order-history lookup taking upward of eight seconds per call instead of its usual under-100-millisecond time.

Every slow call held a database connection open for its full duration, and under load enough connections were tied up simultaneously to starve everything else — the actual cause of the pool-exhaustion symptoms on-call had been treating as root cause.
A schema migration shipped two days earlier had silently dropped an index the query depended on.
Without the index, the order-history query slowed from under 100ms to over eight seconds.
Each slow call held a connection open, and under load that starved the pool — the symptom mistaken for the root cause.
The missing index, not the connection pool, was the actual root cause; both the slow query and the pool exhaustion were downstream symptoms of it.
Raising the pool size only bought headroom, reducing how often the symptom surfaced.
The missing index was added back later that day.
Query time returned to under 100 milliseconds and the connection pileup was eliminated entirely.
The postmortem was explicit that the pool increase was never the fix — the index was.
